core.text: A Latin verb is a stem plus an ending, and the ending says who is doing it. The first endings to learn are those of **the present tense, 3rd person (-t 'he does', -nt 'they do')**, *praesēns indicātīvī, tertia persōna*: *cantat* = she sings, *cantant* = they sing. The vowel before the ending shows the verb's family: *canta-t*, *vide-t*, *pōn-i-t*, *audi-t*.
The 3rd person is anyone you talk about rather than to: he, she, it, they. English adds -s for one person only (*she sings* / *they sing*); Latin changes the ending for both.
One doer: stem + -t. Several: stem + -nt (-unt, -iunt in the 3rd and 4th conjugations). *Est* / *sunt* (is / are) and *it* / *eunt* (goes / go) are the irregular pair to learn.

invented.en: The slaves work, the master sleeps.

core.text: *Vocat* (he calls) and *vocā!* (call!) are one letter apart. A verb with -t states a fact and has a subject you can point to; without the -t, usually with an exclamation mark or a name being addressed, it is an order: *Mēdus Dāvum vocat.* — *Dāvum vocā!*

teach.title: -t for one, -nt for several
teach.say: A Latin verb is a stem with an ending, and the ending says who is doing it. These two are the present tense, 3rd person (-t 'he does', -nt 'they do'): *Mārcus rīdet* — Marcus laughs; *Puerī rīdent* — the boys laugh. No word for ‘he’ or ‘they’ is needed, because the tail already carries it.

teach.title: a-verbs: -at and -ant
teach.say: *Vocāre* (to call) has an a in front of the ending: *vocat*, he calls; *vocant*, they call. This is the largest family of Latin verbs, and its a stays put in front of both endings.

teach.title: e-verbs: -et and -ent
teach.say: *Vidēre* (to see) has an e: *videt*, he sees; *vident*, they see. The two tails are the same as before; only the vowel in front of them has changed, and that vowel is what says which family a verb belongs to.

teach.title: i-verbs: -it and -iunt
teach.say: *Audīre* (to hear) has an i: *audit*, he hears. In the plural that i does not step aside — it is *audiunt*, they hear, with the i still standing in front of -unt.

teach.title: *Est* and *sunt*
teach.say: One pair refuses the pattern and has to be learned as it stands: *est* (is) and *sunt* (are). *Aemilia māter est* — Aemilia is the mother; *Mārcus et Quīntus puerī Rōmānī sunt* — Marcus and Quintus are Roman boys. Even here the -t and the -nt are visible at the end.

teach.title: The singulars rhyme, the plurals do not
teach.say: *Videt* and *dormit* end a single letter apart — an e in one, an i in the other — and both mean one person doing something. Their plurals part company: *vident*, but *dormiunt*. So before you make a verb plural, look at the vowel in front of the -t: in every verb you have met so far an e gives -ent and an i gives -iunt.

more.text: The learner's notes sort verbs by the last letter of the stem instead of by conjugation: a-stems (*flat, flant*), e-stems (*videt, vident*), consonant- or u-stems (*pōnit, pōnunt*; *exstruit, exstruunt*), weak i-stems (*accipit, accipiunt*) and strong i-stems (*venit, veniunt*). The notes treat the i and u of -(i)t and -(u)nt as 'variable vowels' that drop after another vowel — which is why it is *cantat*, not *cantait* — but both stay when i meets u (*accipiunt*, *veniunt*). Irregular *est / sunt* and *it / eunt* take prefixes: *abest*, *adest*, *abit*, *exit*.

No pronoun is needed; the ending carries 'he / she / it / they'. The indicative (*indicātīvus*, the plain statement form) is the mood of facts: statements and questions about what is so. Ørberg cap. IV contrasts indicātīvus -at, -et, -it, -it with imperātīvus -ā, -ē, -e, -ī. The other persons (-ō, -s, -mus, -tis) arrive in cap. XV. A&G §170, §174.
